examples.en: I suffered from a heavy workload and my health got much worse.
My father is always tired because of his heavy workload.
A colleague who collapsed from overwork was admitted to the hospital.

examples.ko: 요즘 격무가 계속돼서 주말에도 쉬지 못해요.
examples.en: The heavy workload continues these days, so I can't rest even on weekends.
The workload was too much to bear, so I moved to another department.

examples.ko: 병원 의사들은 격무 속에서도 환자를 먼저 생각해요.
examples.en: Hospital doctors put patients first even amid a heavy workload.

explain: 일이 많고 힘든 직장 생활에 쓰는 말이에요. 일상 대화에서는 '일이 너무 많아요'라고 하고, '격무'는 뉴스나 글에서 자주 나와요. '격무에 시달리다'로 가장 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is used for a job with a lot of hard work. In daily talk people say '일이 너무 많아요', while '격무' shows up more in news and writing. The most common pattern is '격무에 시달리다'.

examples.ko: 사람들 앞에서 친구를 모욕하면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not humiliate a friend in front of other people.
That customer insulted the staff member.

examples.ko: 외모로 사람을 모욕하는 말은 하지 마세요.
examples.en: Do not say things that insult people for their looks.
I reported the person who insulted me in the comments.
I had no intention of insulting anyone.
After insulting his teacher, he regretted it.

explain: '놀리다'는 장난으로도 쓰지만 '모욕하다'는 상대의 자존심을 심하게 상하게 한다는 느낌이라 훨씬 무거워요. 법에서는 '모욕죄'라고 하고, 일상에서 가볍게 무시할 때는 '무시하다'를 써요.
explain_en: '놀리다' can be playful, but '모욕하다' is much heavier: it means seriously wounding someone's pride. The law has a crime called '모욕죄', and for casually looking down on someone you would use '무시하다'.

examples.en: An unrestrained lifestyle harms your health.
Because of a lack of restraint, my paycheck disappears quickly.
His lack of self-control shows in his credit card bill.
I ate with no restraint and gained weight.
My goal is to cut down on reckless spending.

examples.ko: 무절제한 게임 습관 때문에 늦게 자요.
examples.en: I go to bed late because of my unrestrained gaming habit.

explain: 반대는 '절제'예요. 먹기, 쓰기, 시간 쓰기처럼 조절해야 하는 일을 마음대로 할 때 써요. 주로 '무절제한 + 명사', '무절제하게' 꼴로 쓰고, 말보다 글이나 뉴스에서 더 자주 보여요.
explain_en: Its opposite is '절제' (moderation). It is used when someone does things they should control, such as eating, spending or using time, however they like. It usually appears as '무절제한 + noun' or '무절제하게', and is more common in writing and news than in speech.

examples.ko: 동생이 밉살맞은 표정으로 제 간식을 먹었어요.
examples.en: My younger sibling ate my snack with an irritating look on their face.
That kid is obnoxious in the way they act.
The way they talk is so obnoxious and annoying that I don't even want to answer.
They may look obnoxious, but they're a kind-hearted friend.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 잘난 척을 해서 밉살맞다고 느껴져요.
examples.en: That friend shows off, so they come across as obnoxious.

examples.ko: 밉살맞게 굴던 동료가 오늘은 웬일로 도와줬어요.
examples.en: The coworker who used to be obnoxious surprisingly helped me today.

explain: 하는 말이나 행동이 얄밉고 보기 싫을 때 써요. '밉살스럽다'와 거의 같은 뜻이라 바꿔 쓸 수 있어요. 대화에서는 '얄밉다'도 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is used when someone's words or actions are annoying and hard to stand. It means almost the same as '밉살스럽다', so the two can be swapped. In conversation, '얄밉다' is also widely used.

examples.ko: 길 옆 시궁창에서 심한 냄새가 났어요.
examples.en: A terrible smell came from the gutter by the road.
The ball fell into the ditch and I couldn't get it out.
I want to escape from this gutter of a reality.

examples.ko: 비가 오면 시궁창이 넘쳐서 길이 더러워져요.
examples.en: When it rains, the ditch overflows and the road gets dirty.
There was a sewage smell, so I closed the window.
Cleaning out a ditch is not easy.

explain: 더러운 물이 흘러가는 도랑을 말하고, 일상에서 하수구보다 거칠고 더럽다는 느낌이 강해요. '시궁창 같은 세상'처럼 가장 비참하고 더러운 상황을 비유할 때도 써요. 말투가 거칠어서 격식 있는 자리에서는 조심해요.
explain_en: It refers to a ditch where dirty water flows and feels rougher and filthier than '하수구' (drain). It is also used figuratively for the worst, most miserable situations, as in '시궁창 같은 세상'. The tone is crude, so be careful in formal settings.

examples.ko: 제가 너무 아둔해서 그 뜻을 몰랐어요.
examples.en: I was so slow that I didn't understand what it meant.
He may seem dull, but he is a diligent person.
Thank you for teaching someone as slow as me.
I was foolish to be fooled so easily.
It feels bad to be called dull-witted.
He isn't dull-witted, yet he has no confidence.

explain: 머리 회전이 느리고 눈치가 둔하다는 뜻이라 남에게 쓰면 실례가 될 수 있어요. 그래서 '제가 아둔해서'처럼 자신을 낮출 때 많이 써요. '우둔하다'와 비슷해요.
explain_en: It means slow in thought and dull at picking up on things, so using it about others can be rude. That is why people often use it to humble themselves, as in '제가 아둔해서'. It is similar to '우둔하다'.

examples.en: The key I put down this morning is nowhere to be found.
The cat that was just here was nowhere to be seen.

examples.ko: 온데간데없는 지갑 때문에 하루 종일 찾아다녔어요.
examples.en: I searched all day because of my vanished wallet.
All those people who were here are gone without a trace.

examples.ko: 온데간데없다고 생각한 물건이 가방 속에 있었어요.
examples.en: The thing I thought had vanished was in my bag.
The clothes I used to wear were nowhere to be found, so I asked my mom.

explain: 있던 것이 어디로 갔는지 흔적도 없이 사라졌을 때 써요. 보통 '~이/가 온데간데없다'로 말하고, 한 단어로 붙여 써요. '감쪽같이 사라지다'와 비슷한 느낌이에요.
explain_en: It is used when something that was there has vanished without a trace. It is usually said as '~이/가 온데간데없다' and written as one word. It feels similar to '감쪽같이 사라지다'.

examples.en: When I turned my neck, it made a cracking sound.
Hail rattled down on the roof.
The dry branches snapped with a crack.
I crunched through the nuts.
Big raindrops started pattering down.

examples.ko: 기지개를 켜자 뼈마디에서 우두둑 소리가 났어요.
examples.en: When I stretched, my joints made a cracking sound.

explain: 단단한 것이 부러지거나 뼈마디가 꺾이거나 굵은 빗방울이나 우박이 떨어질 때 나는 소리예요. 소리가 계속될 때는 '우두둑우두둑'이라고 해요. 한 번 부러지는 소리는 '뚝'이 더 자연스러워요.
explain_en: It imitates the sound of something hard snapping, joints cracking, or big raindrops or hail falling. A continued sound is '우두둑우두둑'. For a single snap, '뚝' is more natural.

examples.en: Manual labor is physically very tiring.
My father did manual labor all his life.
You need to rest enough after manual labor.

examples.ko: 저는 사무직보다 육체노동이 더 맞는 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think manual labor suits me better than office work.
We talked about the difference between manual and mental labor.
I tried a manual labor part-time job during vacation.

explain: 몸을 써서 하는 일을 말하고, 반대말은 '정신노동'이에요. 일상에서는 '몸 쓰는 일'이라고도 해요. 직업을 낮춰 보는 말로 들리지 않도록 조심해서 쓰는 게 좋아요.
explain_en: It refers to work done with the body, and its opposite is '정신노동' (mental labor). In daily talk people also say '몸 쓰는 일'. Be careful to use it so it doesn't sound like looking down on a job.

examples.en: Moving boxes for a move is really back-breaking labor.

examples.ko: 중노동을 한 날은 저녁에 바로 잠들어요.
examples.en: On days I do heavy labor, I fall asleep right in the evening.
I suffered from heavy labor from morning till night every day.

examples.ko: 중노동처럼 힘든 청소를 혼자 다 했어요.
examples.en: I did all the grueling cleaning, like hard labor, by myself.
I think even housework is hard labor.

examples.ko: 이 가게는 중노동인데 월급이 너무 적어요.
examples.en: The work at this store is exhausting, but the pay is too low.

explain: 몸을 아주 많이 써야 하는 힘든 일에 써요. 실제 직업 이야기에도 쓰지만, 이삿짐이나 대청소처럼 하루 일이 너무 힘들 때 과장해서 말하기도 해요. '힘든 일'보다 훨씬 강하게 들려요.
explain_en: It is used for work that takes a great deal of physical effort. It can describe real jobs, but people also use it jokingly for tiring days like moving or a big cleaning. It sounds much stronger than just '힘든 일' (hard work).

en: go on a binge; eat too much

examples.en: When I'm stressed, I binge eat without realizing it.
I binged on a late-night meal last night and regretted it.

examples.ko: 다이어트 중에 참다가 결국 폭식을 하고 말았어요.
examples.en: I held out during my diet but ended up bingeing anyway.

examples.ko: 밤마다 이어지는 폭식 때문에 몸무게가 많이 늘었어요.
examples.en: I gained a lot of weight because of nightly binge eating.

examples.ko: 너무 많이 폭식하면 속이 불편하니까 천천히 드세요.
examples.en: If you binge too much your stomach will hurt, so eat slowly.

examples.ko: 시험이 끝난 날 친구와 같이 폭식했어요.
examples.en: On the day the exam ended, I binged with my friend.

explain: '과식하다'는 그냥 많이 먹는 것이고, '폭식하다'는 짧은 시간에 멈추지 못하고 한꺼번에 먹는 느낌이 강해요. '음식을 폭식하다'보다 '폭식을 하다'라고 더 자주 말해요.
explain_en: '과식하다' just means eating too much, while '폭식하다' feels like eating a lot all at once and being unable to stop. People often say '폭식을 하다' rather than putting a food directly before '폭식하다'.

en: lean crop; bad harvest; bad crop

examples.ko: 올해는 가뭄 때문에 사과 농사가 흉작이에요.
examples.en: This year the apple harvest is poor because of the drought.
Because of the bad harvest, rice prices went up a lot.

examples.ko: 태풍이 두 번 지나가서 흉작을 걱정하고 있어요.
examples.en: Two typhoons passed through, so people are worried about a bad harvest.
Last year the harvest was bad, but I hope this year's will be a bumper one.
The bad harvest deepened the farmers' sighs.
I heard the cabbage harvest is bad because of the weather.

explain: 반대말은 '풍작'이고, '흉작이 들다'처럼 많이 써요. 농사 이야기나 뉴스에서 주로 나오고, 일상 대화에서는 '농사가 안 됐어요'라고도 말해요.
explain_en: Its opposite is '풍작' (bumper harvest), and it is often used as '흉작이 들다'. It mostly appears in farming talk and the news, while in daily speech people may also say '농사가 안 됐어요'.
